newsitem.title: CROATIA: Ratings seen boosting Croatia share buying.
newsitem.headline: Ratings seen boosting Croatia share buying.

text.p: Croatia could attract increased foreign investment after it gets a credit rating this month as emerging fund managers switch more money to fresh countries, analysts and traders said on Friday.
"We expect a good year, the interest of international investors is evident," Damir Cikotic at Faktor brokerage told Reuters from the port town of Split.
The local market became a hit in 1996, after two Croatian stocks -- Pliva pharmaceuticals and Zagrebacka Banka -- were listed in London and at home last spring and summer.
Their strong performance sparked a buying interest. As domestic investors joined foreigners, annual turnover jumped 70 times to just under one billion kuna ($180 million).
Trading took off last October, with more firms such as food firms, hotels and shippers coming to the market. That sent prices well above the face value of stocks.
A new bull run which began just after Christmas following a two-month depression, caused partly by concern over President Franjo Tudjman's illness, is seen as lasting for some time.
Unless there are untoward developments to shake the market, traders hope business will consolidate further by Croatia's first sovereign rating from three leading agencies.
They are to pass their assessment, widely expected to be a solid "BB+" or higher, next week.
However, analysts warn a scarcity of liquid new issues and long delays in properly regulating a fledgling capital market, that only got a watchdog last year, might deter future buyers.
"People do want to invest, but not if Croatia proves to be too much hassle," said Milan Elezovic of Nomura Research Institute.
He said a failure by government to boost the securities supply through a wave of fresh privatisation or debt issues might thwart even the best efforts to draw foreign capital.
"What is needed urgently are liquid bank stocks and new debt issues on the state and local levels," said Nened Pavletic at Auctor brokerage.
Croatia was widely praised for the first step made by launching 300 million kuna Eurobonds in December. The bonds are to be listed on the Zagreb Stock Exchange next week.
But traders claim authorities must also see to setting up all missing market institutions, such as a central depository for shares, and removing glitches that halt business.
Although speeded up somewhat after numerous complaints in the past few months, a settlement of well over seven days and sluggish share registering procedure are seen as major problems.
"You buy shares and then wait for papers for a month or so...There is a big risk you may not catch the tide and make money," said one trader with a foreign client base.
He added Pliva and Zagrebacka remained an exception there, lamenting they were the only safe bets for investors now.
Apart from these, trading is done on a fairly regular basis in some 10-15 issues in an environment which lacks reliable data on most companies' performance.
The interest focuses on seaside hoteliers, regaining lost ground on hopes they may be this year's investor pearls as Croatia's tourism industry recovers.
Chocolate maker Kras and food-processor Podravka that may be among next privatisation candidates are also holding well.
